Follow me on my two-month trip through the magic landscapes of South Greenland. Follow me on my deepest journey I’ve ever done so far. On the trails of an ancient legend, Erik the Red. 

From Narsarsuaq, Eriksfjord, Motzfelt Lake, Jespersen Glacier, Igaliku, Tasermiut fjord, Klosterdalen Valley, Ketil, Ulamertorsuaq, Tuppaassat Valley, Kangikitsaq Fjord, Aappilattoq, Itillersuaq Valley, Tasiusaq, to Nanortalik in two months. 

A solo travel journey - a trekking tour, an inner quest to myself. A climbing adventure through South Greenland in August & September 2018.

“I’d like to move. But I can’t. The ice holds me back. Watching infinite beauty for hours. Watch it changing, the shape and colours. I don’t feel anything but great respect. The ice: It quickly draws the eyes under its magic spell. A thousand years it takes to form. A thousand years it takes to move. A thousand years to arrive. I am deeply impressed by the performance of my body and by its rapid adaption to the terrain. Deeply inspired by the landscapes and the lights. I walked between 4.3 billion year old rocks, sometimes covered by the magnificent ice cap. The aurora was above me. Rays seem to touch the earth like an ancient enchanted blessing. Like needles, they descended. Sometimes like blades. One can hear those very strange sounds as long as they dance. A strange noise. Something between the buzz of bees and wind chimes. The stones around me, charged by those lights for thousands of years. Me, so tiny. A blink of an eye in the history of this mountain ridge. I spent hours to watch the stones move, its merger and decay. I had hours listening to the tales from wind and fire. Although I’ve been hurt sometimes, I feel fully alive now. Completely satisfied. My present attention is remarkable and there’s a deep boundary between me and my body. It feels damn good to have it.”
- A.A. September 2018

Greenland  - Since 8 years I'm traveling to this magical country. Today quiet and untouched places are becoming more and more rare. On my first visit to Greenland, I was fascinated by the incredible power of nature that can be felt everywhere. But during the last years things have changed. The amount of icebergs is increasing savagely. Glaciers I'm visiting every year are retreating not meters but kilometers a year and the unending amount of ice seems to be endless. There is nothing more beautiful than an iceberg - everyone is unique and the light reflecting from its surface is magical. It's sad how close beauty and decay can be seen in an iceberg. This movie is is an appreciation to the ice - for me the most amazing aggregate state of water.

Behind the scenes
For this short film I travelled to Greenland with my drones several times. Always with the target of a certain region in a certain light situation. The shots from the calving glacier took me 4 days at the Eqi Glacier and over 70 battery charges for only 4 usable shots of a few seconds. It's a very hard intention to film the very right moment on a glacier front of about 6km wide - especially close up. But the hardest thing of flying in Greenland is the fact, that every 2-3 minutes the difference between the magnetic north and the geographic north (which are not the same place - especially so far north) causing a fatal p-gps flight error and the drone is flying away (also the camera's horizon). But at the end every single flight was worth it - filming Icebergs from above is one of the most beautiful things I've ever done. Additionally I used the drone to scout the landing spot and look for polar bears. The best thing for bears and humans is to not meet each other on shore.

video_title: Armed Forces Radio, live 1963 Thule Greenland T2S1
video_description:
This is one side of several tapes my dad has from Thule Greenland. I transferred these to the computer 20 years ago and I just found the files. On his off time he would record these off the radio with a microphone. This 50:26 recording has a nice announcement at the beginning and an intro for some songs. 20 seconds into the song starting at 42:00, the announcer adds his own touch to the song. I have a few tapes with weather conditions and storm alerts/lockdowns. 

This material is presented as is, for research and relaxing purposes. If allowed by YouTube, I will upload more.

video_title: Armed Forces Radio, live 1963 Thule Greenland (Tape#1
video_description:
Radio announcer talk from the recording of a 4 hour Oldies-But-Goodies-Show from Thule Greenland Armed Forced Radio KBIC 1210 in 1963. My dad taped this off the radio in Thule. There is a cool severe weather warning at the beginning and several song introductions and banter throughout. The images in this video are blank postcards my dad bought at the general store on the base called the Thule Base Exchange.

"Storm Delta" is the most severe Arctic storm classification.  Read more on https://espo.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ATom-4_DeployGuide_THU_final_0.pdf

Nú er bara slétt jökulbreiðan fram undan og þetta verði mun auðveldara. En það varð ekki. Nú birtist hinn grænlenski Kuldaboli sem er stærri og grimmari en sá Íslenski. Kuldinn var kominn í mínus 30°C og átti eftir að vera það meira og minna restina af ferðinni. Reyndar stundum mun meira frost með vindi. Dagleiðirnar lengjast en eru enn stuttar. Við náum ekki upp hraðanum.

video_title: Simulated Greenland Ice Sheet Response Scenario for RCP 2.6: 2008 - 2300
video_description:
Above is a visualization of the Greenland Ice Sheet from 2008 to 2300 is based on the Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 2.6 climate scenario. This is the best case scenario for limiting greenhouse gasses and assumes that emissions will peak by mid-century and decline thereafter. The regions shown in a violet color are exposed areas of the Greenland bed that were covered by the ice sheet in 2008.

The Greenland Ice Sheet holds enough water to raise the world’s sea level by over 7 meters (23 feet). Rising atmosphere and ocean temperatures have led to an ice loss equivalent to over a centimeter increase in global mean sea-level between 1991 and 2015.  Large outlet glaciers, rivers of ice moving to the sea, drain the ice from the interior of Greenland and cause the outer margins of the ice sheet to recede. Improvements in measuring the ice thickness in ice sheets is enabling better simulation of the flow in outlet glaciers, which is key to predicting the retreat of ice sheets into the future.

Recently, a simulation of the effects of outlet glacier flow on ice sheet thickness coupled with improved data and comprehensive climate modeling for differing future climate scenarios has been used to estimate Greenland’s contribution to sea-level over the next millennium. Greenland could contribute 5–34 cm (2-13 inches) to sea-level by 2100 and 11–162 cm (4-64 inches) by 2200, with outlet glaciers contributing 19–40 % of the total mass loss. The analysis shows that uncertainties in projecting mass loss are dominated by uncertainties in climate scenarios and surface processes, followed by ice dynamics. Uncertainties in ocean conditions play a minor role, particularly in the long term. Greenland will very likely become ice-free within a millennium without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

The data sets used for these animations are the control (“CTRL”) simulations and were produced with the open-source Parallel Ice Sheet Model (www.pism-docs.org). All data sets for this study are publicly available at https://arcticdata.io (doi:10.18739/A2Z60C21V).


Visualizers: Cindy Starr (lead), Horace Mitchell, Greg Shirah

For more information or to download this public domain video, go to  https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4721#27356

Large outlet glaciers, rivers of ice moving to the sea, drain the ice from the interior of Greenland and cause the outer margins of the ice sheet to recede.  Improvements in measuring the ice thickness in ice sheets is enabling better simulation of the flow in outlet glaciers, which is key to predicting the retreat of ice sheets into the future.

Recently, a simulation of the effects of outlet glacier flow on ice sheet thickness coupled with improved data and comprehensive climate modeling for differing future climate scenarios has been used to estimate Greenland’s contribution to sea-level over the next millennium. Greenland could contribute 5–34 cm (2-13 inches) to sea-level by 2100 and 11–162 cm (4-64 inches) by 2200, with outlet glaciers contributing 19–40 % of the total mass loss. The analysis shows that uncertainties in projecting mass loss are dominated by uncertainties in climate scenarios and surface processes, followed by ice dynamics.  Uncertainties in ocean conditions play a minor role, particularly in the long term. Greenland will very likely become ice-free within a millennium without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

Now I am preparing a short film about the life of fishermen and hunters in the Arctic of Greenland in climate change times. The idea is to make a film work good enough to be shown at a scientific conference or at a short film festival.

These are two small pieces of more 200 hours that I filmed in different places in northwest Greenland. In one of them, I am walking alone near the Greenland Ice cap in Ikerasak (really cold); I did many long solo walks through mountains and the frozen sea...total silence, stillness everywhere ... except the wind with its grave contralto voice from time to time. In the other one, I'm with two hunters going after narwhal. In a later scene, I head towards the Ice Cap with a renowned Inuit hunter to check the seal traps of the Arctic.

video_title: Contest 01 - Impact of climate change on daily life - Team 04 (Greenland
video_description:
Waste in an indigenous community of the North.

There was a time before consumerism, and a time after. Trash piles up in Uummannaq, as we rely more and more on the modern world. We are thinking about solutions, but there is still a long way to go.

video_title: Contest 01 - Impact of climate change on daily life - Team 06 (Greenland
video_description:
Oil keeps us warm.

In Uummannaq, we need oil to heat our homes. There is no alternative here. Although some people start using solar energy, it is very marginal. This shows the daily life of the people who bring us energy.

video_title: Contest 01 - Impact of climate change on daily life - Team 05 (Greenland
video_description:
After darkness comes the Sun.

When you spend three months without any Sun, the few seconds of Sun light showing on the first Sunny day are magical for the whole town. Today, the Sun is back.

Changing Minds - Greenland Expedition - Episode 1

The summer of 2014.

In South Greenland Tim De Dobbeleer and myself hoped to find our desire to combine climbing big walls with travelling on ourselves, as pure as possible. The massif fjords of South Greenland offer a perfect way to travel by water. Renting a boat would be too expensive, renting a kayak as well. We did some research, contacted some specialists and one impulsive morning Tim and I decided to drive to Amsterdam to buy two new inflatable kayaks in the kayakshop Arjan Bloem. In only three weeks time we prepared and organised this expedition. With limited time to plan, we decided to do further research when we arrived in Greenland, to choose a particular wall.

Enjoy this first episode (of  5) from our Greenland Changing Minds Expedition!

Changing Minds - Greenland Expedition - Episode 5

The Thumbnail is a mighty granite big wall rising straight out of the Torsukattak fjord reaching a height of 1350 meter. This is definitely one of the biggest, maybe ‘the’ biggest, sea cliff in the world. It has been climbed the first time on the far right side of the wall in 2000 by a British team lead by Ian Parnell. Since then three more lines have been climbed on this big wall, but all of them where easier then the British first ascent with the grade E6 6b. The wall has still a lot of first ascent potential and looked like the perfect main objective of our trip.

Changing Minds - Greenland Expedition - Episode 4

Together we cruised down the mountain river in our kayaks with a ton of gear. We were surrounded by the most beautiful mountains, glaciers, rocky fields, flowers, meadows,… in a nutshell: wild nature at its best! Unlike the flat and deep waters of the fjords, kayaking on this shallow and small mountain river in Klosterdalen with a rubber ‘flat-water’ kayak was exciting. We had been sick of hiking!

video_description:
The guardian of the mountains walks along a narrow path high in the peaks. The sun wraps everything in gentle light, and the air is filled with the scent of resin and blooming thyme.
She sings softly, almost in a whisper, yet her voice carries far — old highlander melodies sound purest here. They intertwine with the faint jingle of beads on her attire and the rustle of wind through the grasses.
She lets the music flow freely, for on such an ordinary, warm day the mountains truly need nothing more — only her voice and that quiet, joyful laughter that sometimes breaks through the melody.

video_title: Gigantic Greenland glacier growing after years of melting: NASA
video_description:
녹기만하던 그린란드 빙하의 반전... 얼음이 늘었다

A major glacier in Greenland,... that was one of the fastest shrinking ice and snow masses on Earth is growing again.
However, NASA says the growth is just temporary.
Lee Seung-jae reports. 
This is the Jakobshavn Glacier seen in 2015,... a major mass of ice in Greenland,... considered one of the fastest shrinking ice and snow masses on Earth.
Since 2012, it's been retreating about 3 kilometers and thinning nearly 40 meters annually.
However, a new report by NASA shows the glacier has started growing again.
"Between 2016 and 2017 from two separate NASA airborne missions we found that near the front of the glacier has thickened by up to 30 meters. That's almost a hundred feet in one year and between 2017 and 2018 the same thing again. The difference in the latter year is that this thickening has extended far upstream compared to the 2016 2017 period. So this effect is continuing." 
Scientists say a natural cyclic cooling of North Atlantic waters is the likely cause.
They say the latest regrowth in ice,... coincides with a flip of the North Atlantic Oscillation,... a natural and temporary cooling and warming of parts of the ocean.
While the growth may be welcome news,... experts believe the change is temporary,... and may even be bad news in the long run.
"In the long run it's actually bad news because we demonstrate, this study demonstrates how sensitive this glacier and probably others in Greenland, how sensitive it is to ocean variability and is specifically and particularly the temperature of the ocean." 
In Greenland as a whole,... there's enough ice in the ice sheet to raise global sea levels by seven meters. 
Scientists say they plan to continue observing the latest trends at the Jakobshavn glacier.
Lee Seung-jae, Arirang News.

video_title: Calving Front of Jakobshavn Glacier, Greenland
video_description:
The team flies up the fjord toward the calving front of Jakobshavn glacier, on their way to their field site inland on the ice sheet. Icebergs surrounded by open water transition to mélange (a mixture of sea ice and ice bergs) as the aircraft approaches the front of the glacier.

Credits to twin otter pilot Steindór Jónsson and co-pilot Grétar Benediktsson for their assistance in mounting the GoPro on the plane.

Coordinates: 69.2N,-49.8E

These videos were taken during the spring 2018 iteration of the the NASA-funded project "Towards an Operational System for Estimating Greenland Ice Sheet Thickness Change from Altimetry", developed by BPCRC PI's Ian Howat and Santiago de la Peña. The field campaign included three team members: Santiago de la Peña, and graduate students Michalea King and Sal Candela.

video_title: Northeast Regional View of Simulated Greenland Ice Sheet Response Scenario RCP 2.6: 2008 - 2300
video_description:
Above is a visualization of the northeastern region Greenland Ice Sheet from 2008 to 2300 is based on the Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 2.6 climate scenario. This is the best case scenario for limiting greenhouse gasses and assumes that emissions will peak by mid-century and decline thereafter.  The regions shown in a violet color are exposed areas of the Greenland bed that were covered by the ice sheet in 2008.

The Greenland Ice Sheet holds enough water to raise the world’s sea level by over 7 meters (23 feet). Rising atmosphere and ocean temperatures have led to an ice loss equivalent to over a centimeter increase in global mean sea-level between 1991 and 2015. Large outlet glaciers, rivers of ice moving to the sea, drain the ice from the interior of Greenland and cause the outer margins of the ice sheet to recede. Improvements in measuring the ice thickness in ice sheets is enabling better simulation of the flow in outlet glaciers, which is key to predicting the retreat of ice sheets into the future.

Recently, a simulation of the effects of outlet glacier flow on ice sheet thickness coupled with improved data and comprehensive climate modeling for differing future climate scenarios has been used to estimate Greenland’s contribution to sea-level over the next millennium. Greenland could contribute 5–34 cm (2-13 inches) to sea-level by 2100 and 11–162 cm (4-64 inches) by 2200, with outlet glaciers contributing 19–40 % of the total mass loss. The analysis shows that uncertainties in projecting mass loss are dominated by uncertainties in climate scenarios and surface processes, followed by ice dynamics. Uncertainties in ocean conditions play a minor role, particularly in the long term. Greenland will very likely become ice-free within a millennium without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

The data sets used for these animations are the control (“CTRL”) simulations and were produced with the open-source Parallel Ice Sheet Model (https://pism-docs.org/wiki/doku.php). All data sets for this study are publicly available at the NSF Arctic Data Center (https://arcticdata.io/catalog/view/doi:10.18739/A2Z60C21V).

Visualizers: Horace Mitchell, Greg Shirah, Cindy Starr (lead)

Arctic Char Fly Fishing in Greenland mid July, fishing anytime of the day with no darkness this time of the year. First class fighting fish on light weight rods. Stunning landscapes and wildlife.

Arctic Char Fishing, located North of Greenland away from civilisation, only access to this remote location is via boat travelling through the Fjords.

The Char are some of the hardest fighting fish I have come across, using 6# fly rods stripping the line of the reel with sometimes unto 100 meters in one run.

These fish are migratory running the rivers from early June with hundreds travelling through the river system. 

The location is set within some of the most stunning scenery Greenland has to offer, the fishing does require some long hiking to get to the best fishing areas, but once there you can fish 24/7 and at night under the midnight sun for this time of the year.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the snap election last month, hoping that her straight-talking image in the Greenland crisis would boost her with the electorate. If Frederiksen, the leader of the center-left Social Democratic party can put together a new government, she will embark on her third term. In her second term, Frederiksen's support had waned as the cost of living rose — something that, along with pensions and a potential wealth tax, has been a prominent campaign issue. STORYLINE:
Danish voters went to the polls Tuesday in a general election, with Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen seeking a third term at the helm of the Scandinavian country after a standoff with U.S. President Donald Trump over the future of the kingdom’s semiautonomous territory of Greenland.

More than 4.3 million people are eligible to have their say in the vote for the new Folketing, or parliament, in Copenhagen, which is elected for a four-year term. 

Frederiksen called the election in February, several months before she had to in apparent hopes that her resolute image in the crisis over Greenland would help her with voters in the European Union and NATO member country.

In her second term, her support had waned as the cost of living rose — something that, along with pensions and a potential wealth tax, has been a prominent campaign issue. 

The 48-year-old center-left Social Democrat is known for strong support of Ukraine in its defense against Russia’s invasion and for a restrictive approach to migration — continuing a tradition in Danish politics that now goes back two decades.

Seeking to counter pressure from the right and pointing to a possible surge in migration because of the Iran war, Frederiksen announced proposals this month that include a potential “emergency brake” on asylum and tighter controls on criminals who lack legal residence. Her government had already unveiled a plan to allow the deportation of foreigners who have been sentenced to at least one year in prison for serious crimes.



Further to the right, the anti-immigration Danish People’s Party looks well-placed to bounce back from a very weak showing at the last election in 2022.

All of us have seen Greenland flags, and we can surely recognize at least five. We all know what flags are - they are a piece of women cloth that is often flown from a mast and is generally symbolic in nature.

Greenland flags video are perhaps the most common of all flags. Today, all countries all over the Greenland each have their own flag. The flags of the Nuuk are all unique. Each has its own distinct ways of representing their countries in various aspects. The national flag design usually bears a certain interpretation that is very significant to the country it symbolizes. In general, Greenland flags represent the countries of the Greenland - the number of national flags in existence today is equivalent to the number of nations and countries there are.

National and Greenland Flag History

How did flags come to be? Flag-like symbols have been in existence since the ancient times. It is not clear though where the Nuuk flags that we know today originated. Some say they originated in China, others believe that the first true flag was the vexillum of the RGreenland Empire, while some insist that there have been citations flags in the Mahabharata. While there is no unified origin, the modern-day flag surely had started sometime in the 18th century. Flags have then been used as signals and symbols for battle, military, and maritime purposes, among a few others. Even today, flags are continually used for a wide variety of purposes.

Most Popular video Flags Around the Greenland 

It is true that some flags are more popular than others. Who would not know the Nuukn flag, also known as The Stars and Stripes? Another popular Nuuk flag is that of Denmark in white with the red rising sun in the middle? France's tricolor, Denmark red with five yellow stars, and Greenland's black, red and gold bands are among the most popular flags as well. Some national flags have even been inspirational design-wise to other countries, nations and sub-national entities.

Learning about International Flags

The popularity of the Internet has given way to many accessible resources on Greenland flags. Countless of websites containing flags pictures can be found in the Greenland Wide Web. This makes access to information about the flags of the Greenland very easy nowadays, especially for grade schoolers who probably constitute the majority of those are required to learn about video Greenland flags. Learning about international flags are still a mainstay in primary education mainly because this is one of the most effective ways for kids to learn about the existence of different countries all around the world.

video_description:
Denmark contributes two thirds of Greenland's budget revenue, the rest coming mainly from fishing. Potential oil, gas and rare earth mineral reserves have attracted prospecting firms.

Greenland enjoys perpetual daylight for two months each year but over 80% of the island is covered by an ice cap 4km thick in places. Global warming is feared to be causing the ice cover to melt increasingly fast but has also increased access to Greenland's mineral resources.

The USA has long seen Greenland as strategically important and established a radar base at Thule at the start of the Cold War.

The island's population is only 57,000, and Greenlanders have long struggled with social problems - not least among them the impact of alcoholism and HIV/AIDS.

https://www.dancingwiththesea.com/

This video series is all about giving you the quickest way to get a major breakthrough in your skill level. Even if you’ve have been kayaking for many years, and it seems like you’re not gonna get any better.

It’s for you if you want sea kayaking to feel safe. Know that you can avoid capsizing. Maybe  you want paddling to feel nice and easy. Relaxing. If your arms and shoulders feel sore or tired after a day of paddling, you may want to put an end to that. Maybe even have more speed so you can stop feeling like you have to struggle to keep up. Especially if you are holding your friends back.  Ultimately you want to have the freedom to go where you want, with whom you want. The possibility to experience life changing adventures.

Did you know that it’s possible to have that in a few months? It doesn’t have to take years.

I really want to be clear about this. It’s not how long you practice. It’s what you do differently. 

I discovered something, from watching a rolling demonstration by a young Inuit, that would change this very quickly. When I got it, I couldn’t believe that no one else is doing this. It gave me more than enough speed to keep up with even the stronger paddlers. I quickly learned how to roll with such ease that capsizing became irrelevant. But I didn’t need to roll anymore because I didn’t capsize. With my newly gained agility, I was solid in the waves. 
It made everything I do with my kayak so much easier. And nobody is teaching this. That’s what inspired me to create DancingWithTheSea.com 

It’s a place where anyone can learn the techniques that were designed to work with the sea kayak.

When the Inuit make a kayak, they include something called a masik. 
It lets the paddler do something most kayaks don’t allow. At least not until you adjust the kayak to fit you properly.

A masik is basically a piece of wood that goes over your legs., above the knees.

You don’t need that for the techniques most people are teaching. And that’s why nobody talks about it. 

Most kayakers use techniques made for river kayaking. Not what the Inuit figured out over thousands of years. And it’s really a different feeling. 

The euro blade may be good for river kayaking, or for the olympics. But you may be the kind of person who wants paddling to feel easier, and smoother. Maybe you don’t want to use force. You may want  more of the peace of mind that comes from having the skills to stay upright in any conditions. That’s when you really start to enjoy kayaking. 

The Greenland style is perfect for that. 

In order for the rest of the world to know the benefits of these techniques, I created the training website DancingWithTheSea.com

Join me for the next video where I show you the steps you need to quickly develop these skills. It’s not about years of practice I promise you. But there are a few things you need to understand before you can be agile with your kayak.

I’ll see you in the next video.


In the next video I’ll show you why the masik is what separates the kayak from every other boats. And why it’s the key to developing kayak mastery.

ILLUSTRATED GUIDE: One Simple Movement Makes You Stable In Waves (With Before/After Demonstrations):  https://www.dancingwiththesea.com/op/stable/?video=qMzmCQBOSUE

I see people practicing for years without much improvement.

I’ll show you why that’s happening in this video.

The philosophy is very simple. Instead of using strength and a big blade, we use our body in a natural way, to make all the techniques feel easy. No fighting against the water. That’s why I call it dancing with the sea. 


Here’s some good news.

Although it may seem like you need to fix your forward stroke, learn to brace so you can be more secure in the waves, learn to roll, edge, turn, I will show you how mastering all those skills is really about getting good at just a few things.  And it’s not even hard when you know what to do. 

It will all make sense in a few minutes.

Like I mentioned in the first video the Inuit designed the kayak with a masik. In my opinion, this is what distinguishes the kayak from a boat. You can sit in a boat and paddle it, but only a kayak can be worn. I know a lot of people will argue that what makes the kayak is the shape or the double blade. But only wearing your kayak will give you that agility on the water. Agility which only the kayak can give you. That’s the true genius of the kayak in my mind. 

Your hips are made to move this way. Forward and back. When you move from side to side, you can only bend your spine. Your hips just don’t move that way. Not much range of motion there.

When you don’t rotate in your kayak, you can only move your body forward and back. Sideways you are kind of limited. When you rotate you gain the range of motion that gives you power, and also agility. 

Power for your forward stroke, to go faster. It’s also what gives you the endurance to go the distance. To explore more out of the way wilderness areas.

The extra range of motion makes it easy to avoid a capsize.

Support is really built into your forward stroke so you never have to worry about getting out of balance. Now you have a powerful position for edging and turning in the waves without ending up in the water. 

When rolling a kayak most people do it without using the flexibility in their hips. They just use their upper body, and strength and coordination. That’s why it’s so hard for most people to learn. And why it’s considered an advanced skill. For the Inuit it was the first thing they learned to do in a kayak. It’s actually easy when you rotate your hips to get that extra range of motion. 


So the most important thing you can do to improve any skill you learn with your kayak has nothing to do with practice. It has everything to do with learning to move with your kayak.

I’ll show you how in the next video, see you there.

video_title: EF Google Videos. Narsaq, Greenland. 27 Julio 2017
video_description:
Visita al puerto de Narsaq, Greenland, como parte del recorrido del Crucero HAL “25 días de Leyendas Nórdicas y Travesía Vikinga” que nos llevó desde Rotterdam a Boston. 02 de julio a 02 agosto 2017.
El programa de este dia era hacer el cruising del Prince Christian Sund; pero estaba bloquedo por el hielo, de manera que tuvimos que cambiar, no solo la ruta para llegar a Qaqortoq (navegamos por el Skove Fjord), sino también sustituir el próximo puerto previsto, Nanortalik, por el de Narsaq. 
This harbour is only open from May to October. Narsaq is a town in the Kujalleq municipality in southern Greenland. The name Narsaq is Greenlandic for “plain”, referring to the beautiful plain on the shore of Tunulliarfik Fjord where the town is located. With 1,613 inhabitants as of 2010, it is the ninth-largest town in Greenland. This is a useful Port of Entry for Greenland if coming from Southeast Labrador.
Narsaq is a town in southern Greenland, and the Narsaq Sound is always full of icebergs of all shapes and sizes.
Fishing is the mainstay of the local economy. Local fjords are full of marine life, including whales, salmon, and seals. Uniquely in Greenland, farming is possible on the plains to the north of the town, with several actively maintained arable fields. Of the 53 registered sheep farms in Greenland, 31 are located in the Narsaq area. The farms produce meat for domestic consumption, and the Narsaq slaughterhouse Neqi A/S, a wholly owned subsidiary of KNI, is the only slaughterhouse in the country. The sheep farming area of Tasiusaq is located in former Norse area. The third major part of the economy is tourism. South Greenland has experienced a decline in tourist revenue in recent years, but tourism still supports a significant percentage of the viable workforce. Popular activities include hiking, fishing, collecting rare minerals and taking boat trips to the ice cap.

🇩🇰 🇬🇱Denmark, Greenland Island

The island of Greenland is the largest on Earth, located in the north-east direction from North America, washed by three large bodies of water: The Arctic Ocean in the north, the Labrador Sea on the south side and the Baffin Sea on the west side. To date, the island territory belongs to Denmark.

Greenland is a rare place that has been preserved as untouched as possible, and human intervention is minimal. There are excellent conditions for extreme sports, ecotourism, which is popular today. Nature lovers can admire the amazing landscapes, plunge into the original culture of the peoples inhabiting the island, who still live according to ancient traditions. The length of Greenland from north to south is almost 2.7 thousand km, the maximum width is about 1.3 thousand km, and the area is 2.2 thousand square kilometers, which is 50 times the area of Denmark.

video_description:
Explore Ilulissat, Greenland with me in this walk-and-talk video as I walk through the streets of this charming city of Ilulissat, Greenland. 

Ilulissat means Icebergs. It has the biggest icebergs you'll see outside Antarctica. Ilulissat Icebergs come from Jakobshavn Glacier known as Ilulissat glacier, which is the world’s fasted glacier and moves up to 40 meters per day. The iceberg that sank the Titanic was probably born in Ilulissat. Ilulissat was founded in 1741. The population is approximately 4530.

The midnight sun lasts between 27 May and 18 July. The sun never sets on the town of Ilulissat during this period. This experience, known as the Midnight Sun, only occurs above the Arctic Circle.

Discover the extraordinary story of the Aviationtag Norsaq – a piece of aviation history that transcends its role as an aircraft and embodies the essence of Greenlandic connection and adventure. Norsaq, an Airbus A330-200 with the registration OY-GRN and MSN 230, was originally delivered to Sabena in 1998 before joining Air Greenland's fleet in August 2002. Serving as a vital link between Greenland and Denmark for over two decades, Norsaq has not only transported passengers but has become a symbol of shared experiences and a conduit for countless adventures.

From charter trips to southern Europe to facilitating the participation of Greenlandic athletes in international events, Norsaq's legacy is rich with diverse journeys. It has even hosted live bands, witnessed weddings, and remained a cherished symbol of travel for generations in Greenland.

With 41,364 flying hours and 10,112 take-offs and landings, Norsaq found its final resting place on March 12, 2023, concluding a remarkable chapter. As part of its farewell journey to Arizona, Air Greenland orchestrated a special flight, making a unique loop over Nuuk, Greenland's capital, bidding a poignant goodbye.

Now, as an Aviationtag, Norsaq's story lives on. Own a piece of this aviation legacy – a keychain or luggage tag that transcends its utilitarian function, becoming a tangible connection to the remarkable journey of Norsaq.

video_title: How Do Greenlanders Survive Brutal Winter?
video_description:
How Do Greenlanders Survive Brutal Winter? Winter in Greenland is not a season that arrives gently. It descends early, lingers long, and reshapes every aspect of daily life. For months, temperatures remain far below freezing, daylight fades into prolonged darkness, and storms can isolate entire communities. Yet people continue to live, work, raise families, and maintain routines in conditions many would consider uninhabitable. Understanding how Greenlanders endure this environment reveals a story of preparation, cultural knowledge, social resilience, and deep adaptation to nature rather than resistance against it.

1. Homes Built to Hold Heat and Resist the Arctic
Housing in Greenland is engineered around one central priority: retaining warmth in a relentlessly cold environment. Buildings are compact, heavily insulated, and designed to minimise exposure to wind and drifting snow. Thick walls, triple-glazed windows, and sealed entryways help prevent heat loss, while raised foundations protect structures from shifting ice and seasonal ground movement. Many homes are arranged to reduce surface area exposed to the elements, which lowers heating demands. Bright exterior colours are common, not for decoration, but to improve visibility during storms and long periods of low light. Inside, layouts prioritise warmth efficiency, often concentrating living spaces together so heat circulates effectively. Heating systems are not optional comforts but life-sustaining infrastructure. District heating networks, fuel reserves, and backup systems are standard in towns. Even in smaller settlements, heating reliability is treated as essential, because loss of warmth in winter can quickly become dangerous. These housing choices are not recent innovations but the result of decades of adaptation to Arctic conditions.

2. Clothing as a Survival Strategy, Not a Style Choice
In Greenland, winter clothing functions as a protective system rather than a fashion statement. Every layer serves a purpose, working together to manage body heat, moisture, and wind exposure. The principle is simple: stay dry, trap warmth, and block wind. Traditional designs, informed by Inuit knowledge, emphasise insulation and mobility. Fur-lined hoods protect the face from freezing winds, while layered garments trap air close to the body. Modern materials have been added over time, but the logic remains unchanged. Clothing must perform during long periods outdoors, often without the option to seek shelter quickly. Footwear is particularly important. Boots are built to insulate against ice while allowing circulation to prevent frostbite. Gloves, head coverings, and face protection are treated as essential equipment rather than accessories. Dressing correctly is not about comfort alone; it is a matter of safety and endurance in an environment where exposure can quickly become hazardous.

3. Food Choices Designed for Cold and Energy
Winter in Greenland limits agriculture and restricts supply routes, shaping a diet focused on energy, preservation, and local availability. Food is chosen for its ability to sustain the body through prolonged cold rather than for variety or novelty. Traditional winter foods rely heavily on fish and other locally sourced resources that store well and provide dense nutrition. High-fat and high-protein foods are particularly valuable because they support body heat and physical stamina. Preservation methods such as freezing, drying, and fermenting are widely used, taking advantage of the natural cold rather than fighting it. Imported foods are available in larger towns, but reliance on them decreases during harsh winter periods. Households plan carefully, stocking supplies well in advance of storms or transport disruptions. Meals are often communal, reinforcing social bonds while ensuring that everyone has access to adequate nutrition during the most demanding months of the year.

video_title: 12 Daily Challenges That Define Life In Greenland
video_description:
What are the 12 daily challenges that define life in Greenland? Life in Greenland is shaped less by choice and more by reality. Geography, climate, and distance quietly dictate how days unfold, how plans are made, and how people think about comfort, time, and community. This is not a place built around speed or convenience. It is a place where adjustment becomes instinct and patience becomes routine. From the way people travel to how they shop, heat their homes, and stay connected, life here follows rules written by nature. These are not occasional difficulties—they are daily conditions. Ranked from twelve to one, here are the everyday challenges that truly define life in Greenland.

12. Planning Everything Around the Weather
Weather is not small talk in Greenland; it is the organising force behind daily life. A clear sky in the morning offers no guarantees by afternoon. Strong winds can rise without warning, snow can thicken visibility in minutes, and fog can cancel transport entirely. People learn early not to anchor plans too tightly. Appointments, school schedules, work commitments, and social gatherings all bend around weather conditions.
This constant unpredictability shapes mindset. Instead of frustration, there is acceptance. People check forecasts carefully, but they also expect them to be wrong. Outdoor work pauses when conditions turn unsafe. Boats stay docked. Flights are delayed or cancelled without drama. Over time, flexibility replaces expectation. In life in Greenland, the weather always has the final say, and resisting that fact only makes the day harder.

11. Limited Transportation Between Towns
Greenland has no road network linking its towns. Each settlement exists as a self-contained pocket along the coast or deep within fjords. Travel between them happens by air, sea, or sled depending on season. In summer, boats connect communities. In winter, helicopters and small planes take over. Bad weather can shut everything down. This reality changes how people perceive distance. A neighbouring town may be physically close but practically unreachable for days. Missed connections are normal, not exceptional. Travel plans are built with buffers, patience, and contingency. Everyday life in Greenland includes the understanding that movement is a privilege granted by conditions, not a right guaranteed by infrastructure.

10. Long Periods Without Sunlight
In winter, many parts of Greenland experience weeks where the sun never rises. The darkness is complete and constant. Streetlights stay on all day. Homes glow warmly from within. Life continues, but the absence of daylight subtly affects rhythm and energy. People adapt by creating structure indoors. Work routines remain steady. Social visits become important. Homes are designed to feel cosy, not spacious. Lighting matters. Candles, warm colours, and familiar routines replace natural cues. Rather than fighting the darkness, people learn to live alongside it. In life in Greenland, winter is not something to escape—it is something to endure calmly.

9. High Cost of Everyday Goods
Almost everything consumed in Greenland arrives by ship or plane. That reality is reflected in prices. Groceries, household items, clothing, and electronics all cost significantly more than in most countries. Fresh produce is especially expensive and limited. This changes shopping habits entirely. People plan meals carefully and waste very little. Bulk buying, freezing, and rationing are normal. Local foods such as fish and game play an important role, not for tradition alone but for affordability. Budget awareness becomes part of daily thinking. In living in Greenland, money stretches differently, and every purchase is considered.

8. Isolation From the Rest of the World
Greenland’s remoteness is physical, not metaphorical. International travel involves multiple connections and long waits. Global trends arrive slowly, if at all. News cycles feel distant. This isolation shapes perspective. People rely heavily on local networks rather than outside systems. Community events matter. Relationships carry weight. There is less pressure to keep up with the outside world and more focus on immediate surroundings. While isolation can feel heavy at times, it also creates clarity. Life in Greenland encourages attention to what is present rather than what is elsewhere.

From the way people travel to how they shop, heat their homes, and stay connected, life here follows rules written by nature. These are not occasional difficulties—they are daily conditions. Ranked from twelve to one, here are the everyday challenges that truly define life in Greenland.

12. Planning Everything Around the Weather
Weather is not small talk in Greenland; it is the organising force behind daily life. A clear sky in the morning offers no guarantees by afternoon. Strong winds can rise without warning, snow can thicken visibility in minutes, and fog can cancel transport entirely. People learn early not to anchor plans too tightly. Appointments, school schedules, work commitments, and social gatherings all bend around weather conditions.
This constant unpredictability shapes mindset. Instead of frustration, there is acceptance. People check forecasts carefully, but they also expect them to be wrong. Outdoor work pauses when conditions turn unsafe. Boats stay docked. Flights are delayed or cancelled without drama. Over time, flexibility replaces expectation. In life in Greenland, the weather always has the final say, and resisting that fact only makes the day harder.

11. Limited Transportation Between Towns
Greenland has no road network linking its towns. Each settlement exists as a self-contained pocket along the coast or deep within fjords. Travel between them happens by air, sea, or sled depending on season. In summer, boats connect communities. In winter, helicopters and small planes take over. Bad weather can shut everything down. This reality changes how people perceive distance. A neighbouring town may be physically close but practically unreachable for days. Missed connections are normal, not exceptional. Travel plans are built with buffers, patience, and contingency. Everyday life in Greenland includes the understanding that movement is a privilege granted by conditions, not a right guaranteed by infrastructure.

10. Long Periods Without Sunlight
In winter, many parts of Greenland experience weeks where the sun never rises. The darkness is complete and constant. Streetlights stay on all day. Homes glow warmly from within. Life continues, but the absence of daylight subtly affects rhythm and energy. People adapt by creating structure indoors. Work routines remain steady. Social visits become important. Homes are designed to feel cosy, not spacious. Lighting matters. Candles, warm colours, and familiar routines replace natural cues. Rather than fighting the darkness, people learn to live alongside it. In life in Greenland, winter is not something to escape—it is something to endure calmly.

9. High Cost of Everyday Goods
Almost everything consumed in Greenland arrives by ship or plane. That reality is reflected in prices. Groceries, household items, clothing, and electronics all cost significantly more than in most countries. Fresh produce is especially expensive and limited. This changes shopping habits entirely. People plan meals carefully and waste very little. Bulk buying, freezing, and rationing are normal. Local foods such as fish and game play an important role, not for tradition alone but for affordability. Budget awareness becomes part of daily thinking. In living in Greenland, money stretches differently, and every purchase is considered.

8. Isolation From the Rest of the World
Greenland’s remoteness is physical, not metaphorical. International travel involves multiple connections and long waits. Global trends arrive slowly, if at all. News cycles feel distant. This isolation shapes perspective. People rely heavily on local networks rather than outside systems. Community events matter. Relationships carry weight. There is less pressure to keep up with the outside world and more focus on immediate surroundings. While isolation can feel heavy at times, it also creates clarity. Life in Greenland encourages attention to what is present rather than what is elsewhere.

Despite these tensions and external pressures, including United States interest in the island, the overall alliance between Greenland and Denmark remains stable.

Welcome to the first 24/7 4K livestream from the breathtaking waters of Ilulissat, Greenland!

Immerse yourself in the stunning Arctic scenery as we capture the ever-changing beauty of towering icebergs, the pristine ocean, and fascinating wildlife. From drifting ice giants to seabirds, seals, and the occasional whale sighting, there's always something magical to see.

You can experience this exact view in person by staying at this beautiful ocean front home in Ilulissat, Greenland.  This home is located in one of the absolute best locations in Ilulissat, where you can hear the sea just outside as well as the smell of the ice from Ilulissat Isfjord. Learn more here: https://www.ilulissatstay.com/en/jomsborg-ilulissat

------
About the Ilulissat Icefjord:

The Ilulissat Icefjord is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and home to Sermeq Kujalleq (aka: Jakobshavn Glacier or Ilulissat Glacier), one of the world’s most active glaciers. This glacier produces a staggering 35 billion tons of ice annually, creating colossal icebergs that drift into the ocean. Some of these icebergs are so massive they can take years to melt, and it’s believed that one may have even been the iceberg that sank the Titanic! 

What makes the Icefjord truly awe-inspiring is its dynamic landscape—icebergs cracking, shifting, and shimmering under the Arctic light, with colors ranging from bright white to deep, translucent blues.

------
 Marine Life You Might Spot:

The rich, cold waters around Ilulissat are teeming with Arctic wildlife. Keep your eyes peeled for:

* Whales: Humpback, minke, and fin whales are commonly seen, especially in the summer months.
* Seals: You might spot ringed seals and harp seals resting on the ice or swimming gracefully in the water.
* Birdlife: Look out for Arctic terns, gulls, fulmars, and other seabirds soaring above the waves.
* Occasional Surprises: Polar bears are rare in this area, but sometimes venture onto drifting ice floes.

------
How you can help!

If you see an accident at sea: someone with boat trouble, a person or animal in distress, please let us know! Post it on chat with a timestamp.  If it is clearly serious, please contact the Joint Rescue Coordination Center (JRCC) Greenland: https://eng.navigation.gl/rescue-service
Thanks!

-----
🏘️ Discover Ilulissat – The Town at the Edge of Ice:

Ilulissat, meaning “Icebergs” in Greenlandic, is the third-largest town in Greenland with around 4,500 residents. Despite its small size, it’s rich in culture and history. Founded in 1741, Ilulissat is the birthplace of famed polar explorer Knud Rasmussen. The colorful houses, friendly locals, and a vibrant mix of traditional Inuit culture with modern Arctic life make it a fascinating place to explore. Plus, it’s one of the best places on Earth to witness the midnight sun in summer and the magical northern lights in winter! 

------
📸 What You’ll Experience:

* Majestic icebergs from the Ilulissat Icefjord
* Arctic marine wildlife in their natural habitat
* The serene sounds of the Arctic Ocean
* Views of Ilulissat’s dramatic Arctic landscape
* Spectacular sunrises, sunsets, and seasonal light changes

------
🌐 Perfect For:

* Relaxation and meditation
* Nature lovers and ocean enthusiasts
* Ambient background for your day

Victor Davis Hanson is a renowned classicist, military historian, and political commentator. Victor most recently appeared on episode #231, which came out just before the 2024 election, and where he made a case to vote for Donald Trump. video_title: Mega tsunamis in Greenland fjord confirmed as source of nine-day global seismic signal
video_description:
Here we discusses the discovery of a global seismic signal originating from Greenland. Specifically, two large landslides in Dickson Fjord in September 2023 generated tsunamis that led to a long-lasting seiche, a standing wave, within the fjord. This seiche was the confirmed source of persistent, ultra-low frequency seismic vibrations detected worldwide for nine days. Researchers were able to directly observe this phenomenon using NASA's SWOT satellite mission, offering new understanding of how surface water motion in remote coastal areas can impact global seismic activity.
Mega tsunamis in Greenland fjord confirmed as source of nine-day global seismic signal
A persistent, ultra-low frequency seismic vibration was detected worldwide in September 2023 and traced to Dickson Fjord, East Greenland, after two large landslides triggered tsunamis and a long-lasting seiche. For the first time, researchers directly observed this standing wave using NASA’s SWOT satellite mission, providing new insights into the connection between global seismic signals and surface water motion in remote coastal environments.
Seismic sensors around the world picked up a persistent, ultra-low frequency vibration at 10.88 millihertz in September 2023 that lasted for 9 days and came back a month later. These very-long-period (VLP) seismic signals were eventually traced back to a remote fjord in East Greenland, where two massive landslides had caused tsunamis.
The real source of the vibration was confirmed to be a seiche bouncing back and forth inside the fjord, an inference based on satellite observations and seismic correlation.

video_title: Scientists Race To Study Greenland Melt That Could Disrupt Atlantic Ocean Currents
video_description:
Scientists are heading to Greenland to investigate a potential climate tipping point that could affect the entire North Atlantic.

Rapid glacier melt is sending large amounts of freshwater into the ocean. That freshwater may interfere with a major Atlantic circulation system that helps regulate temperatures across Europe and North America.

Researchers are deploying drones, robotic submarines, satellites and glacier sensors to monitor the process directly inside Greenland’s fjords.

Some projections suggest major circulation changes could begin as early as the 2040s.

video_title: Every Map You've Ever Seen Has Been Lying To You…😱🗺️ | The Truth About Greenland & Africa
video_description:
You have been looking at a lie your entire life. 🗺️ Hanging on classroom walls. 😶 Printed in every textbook. 📚
Displayed on every phone, every atlas, every geographical reference you have ever consulted. 😳 The world map that humanity has accepted as standard for over 450 years is not accurate. 😤
Not even close. 😱 Meet the Mercator Projection. 🗺️
Created by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 for an extremely specific and completely legitimate purpose — helping sailors navigate using straight line compass routes. 🧭
It was brilliant for that. ⚓ It was never meant for anything else. 😶
But somehow it became THE map. 🌍 The default map. 😤
The classroom map. 📚 The map that shaped how billions of human beings understand the relative size and importance of every country and continent on earth. 😳
And it distorts everything. 😱 Especially near the poles. 🌊
Here is what your map has been telling you about Greenland. 🇬🇱
Greenland appears roughly the same size as Africa on a standard Mercator map. 😳
Sometimes larger. 😱 Here is the truth. 😤 Africa is 14 times larger than Greenland. 😱 Fourteen. Times. 🌍
Africa contains 30.3 million square kilometers. 🌍 Greenland contains 2.1 million square kilometers. 🧊 Inside the actual size of Africa you could fit. 😳
The United States. 🇺🇸
China. 🇨🇳
India. 🇮🇳
Europe. 🌍
Japan. 🇯🇵
And still have room left. 😤 All of them. Simultaneously. Inside Africa. 🌍
And your map makes Africa and Greenland look roughly equal. 🗺️
The Mercator Projection inflates land masses near the poles — making Greenland, Russia, Canada and Alaska appear dramatically larger than they actually are — while compressing land masses near the equator — making Africa, South America, India and Southeast Asia appear dramatically smaller than they actually are. 😰
Which means the map that shaped your entire geographical worldview has been systematically making the Global North look bigger. 😶
And the Global South look smaller. 😤
For 450 years. 📅
This is not a conspiracy. 😶 It is mathematics. 🔢 The mathematics of projecting a spherical planet onto a flat surface — something that is geometrically impossible to do without distortion. 🌍➡️🗺️
Every flat map distorts something. 😳 The Mercator projection distorts size. 📏
And humanity chose it as the default. 😤 There are better projections. 🗺️
The AuthaGraph. 📐 The Winkel Tripel. 🗺️
The Peters Projection specifically designed to preserve accurate land area. 📏

Displayed on every phone, every atlas, every geographical reference you have ever consulted. 😳 The world map that humanity has accepted as standard for over 450 years is not accurate. 😤
Not even close. 😱 Meet the Mercator Projection. 🗺️
Created by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 for an extremely specific and completely legitimate purpose — helping sailors navigate using straight line compass routes. 🧭
It was brilliant for that. ⚓ It was never meant for anything else. 😶
But somehow it became THE map. 🌍 The default map. 😤
The classroom map. 📚 The map that shaped how billions of human beings understand the relative size and importance of every country and continent on earth. 😳
And it distorts everything. 😱 Especially near the poles. 🌊

Sometimes larger. 😱 Here is the truth. 😤 Africa is 14 times larger than Greenland. 😱 Fourteen. Times. 🌍

video_title: WCEE Emerging Issues Lecture. Why Greenland Matters Now
video_description:
Gabriella Gricius, Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Konstanz, Senior Fellow at the Arctic Institute, and Fellow at the North American and Arctic Defence and Security Network

Recorded on March 10, 2026.

Greenland and the wider circumpolar Arctic are no longer peripheral concerns to observers of geopolitics, but are now central sites of geopolitical, economic, and environmental contestation. Focusing on Greenland, the lecture traces how debates over military basing, mineral extraction, Indigenous self-determination, and environmental protection have become tightly intertwined. These overlapping pressures have produced new frictions between Washington, Copenhagen, Brussels, and Nuuk, revealing that Arctic security today is not only about hard security, but also about trade, governance, and competing visions of identity and sovereignty. The lecture will situate the current drama on Greenland in the context of changes in Arctic security as a whole. The lecture will show that Greenland offers a critical lens through which to understand broader shifts in Arctic order: how alliances adapt, how local actors navigate external pressures, and how environmental change is transforming what “security” means in the twenty-first-century Arctic.

Dr. Gabriella Gricius is a Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Konstanz and a Fellow and the Media Coordinator with the North American and Arctic Defence and Security Network (NAADSN). She is also a Senior Fellow at the Arctic Institute. At the University of Konstanz, she is currently working on Nordic security community formation and hybrid threats in the European Arctic region.

She received her PhD from Colorado State University's Political Science Department where her dissertation explored the prevalence of low-tension discourse in Greenland, Svalbard, the Northern Sea Route, and the Northwest Passage. Her writing is published in Foreign Policy, International Politics, European Security, amongst other outlets, and she has also been interviewed by BBC, the New York Times, and other major news outlets.

video_title: Why America is Obsessed with Buying Greenland
video_description:
Imagine an island so vast it could swallow Mexico, Saudi Arabia, and Indonesia combined, yet so cold that only 57,000 people dare to call it home. To most of the world, it is a silent, frozen wasteland. But to the most powerful nations on Earth, it is a gold mine, a shield, and a potential spark for a major global conflict. Why was the President of the United States willing to risk a diplomatic crisis to buy a giant block of ice?

In this video, we dive deep into the geopolitics of Greenland, exploring why this autonomous territory under the Kingdom of Denmark has become the center of a high-stakes power struggle between the U.S., Russia, and China.

The Ultimate Watchtower: National Security
Looking at the globe from the top, Greenland sits directly between North America and Russia. During the Cold War, the U.S. realized its strategic importance for missile defense. Today, the Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule Air Base) houses advanced radar systems that can detect Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles (ICBMs) the moment they launch. Without Greenland, the U.S. mainland would be vulnerable to strikes from the North. This is why, as far back as 1946, President Harry Truman offered Denmark $100 million in solid gold for the island.

The Treasure Under the Frost: Rare Earth Elements
Greenland is not just ice. Hidden beneath its 2-kilometer-thick ice sheet lies one of the world's largest untapped reserves of Rare Earth Elements (REE). These minerals, such as Neodymium and Gallium, are the "oxygen" of modern technology—essential for everything from electric vehicles and wind turbines to AI chips and advanced radar. Currently, China controls nearly 90% of the global supply. For the U.S., controlling Greenland is the key to breaking this monopoly and securing the future of Western technology.

The New Global Trade Route: The Northwest Passage
Climate change is causing Arctic ice to melt at an unprecedented rate. This is opening the Northwest Passage, a sea route that could revolutionize global trade. By sailing through the Arctic instead of the Suez or Panama Canals, cargo ships traveling from Asia to Europe could save 9,000 kilometers and up to 15 days of travel. Greenland sits at the very entrance of this new global highway. Whoever controls the island becomes the "Gatekeeper" of the world’s most important future trade route.
Oil, Cables, and Diplomatic Tension
The stakes don't end with minerals and shipping. Survey results suggest there are over 31 billion barrels of oil off the coast of Greenland. Furthermore, the island is a critical junction for the undersea cables that provide internet connectivity between America and Europe. We examine the tension between the U.S. and Denmark, a key NATO ally, and the desire of the local Greenlandic population for independence and cultural preservation.

In this video, you will learn about:
The history of U.S. attempts to purchase Greenland (Truman to Trump).
The technical importance of the Upgraded Early Warning Radar (UEWR).
The "Rare Earth" mineral war between the US and China.
How global warming is transforming Arctic shipping and the Northwest Passage.
The potential for Greenland to become the flashpoint for "World War 3."
If you are fascinated by international relations, military strategy, and resource exploration, this deep dive into the icy mystery of Greenland is a must-watch!
